risk.line: HIGH, held for an ELEVENTH consecutive pass, and the afternoon supplied the sentence that explains why the gate has not fired. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree declared that maritime navigation in the Red Sea 'is safe, except for Saudi ships' - hours after Ansar Allah completed its takeover of Yemen's entire western coast, taking Dhubab, the Hanish group, Zuqar and Perim and claiming 5,400 square kilometres in under twenty-four hours. That is not a blockade announcement; it is a customer list. A force that intended to close Bab el-Mandeb does not publish a safe-conduct for everyone except one buyer, and a force that wanted the US Navy back in the lane would not have bothered. The gate remains a struck US-flagged merchant hull with a crew aboard, or a confirmed American death, and neither happened. On the pipeline the loudest claim shrank under measurement: the Payne Institute at the Colorado School of Mines, using VIIRS Nightfire from Suomi NPP and the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites, found that at least two KNOWN flares along the East-West line entered an apparent emergency regime on 10-11 September, flow jumping to roughly 0.32-0.44 billion cubic metres a year, and stated plainly that the data do 'not indicate new fires at unusual or previously uncatalogued locations' - which is what a pressure relief looks like, not eight rupture points. Diplomatically the week's real instrument is now dated: Gulf foreign ministers meet Iran's Abbas Araghchi in Salalah on Monday. On the money board August CPI printed 3.4 per cent against a 3.3 per cent consensus with core at 0.3 per cent on the month, diesel set a record above $6 a gallon, and the ten-year pulled back from 5 per cent - a reprieve for the Treasury's funding calendar that changes nothing about the energy pass-through the FOMC has to write down on Wednesday.

forecasts.q: Saudi Aramco or the Saudi authorities publicly confirm a force majeure at Yanbu, Jizan or Ras Tanura, OR a reduction in East-West (Petroline) pipeline throughput, before 31 Dec 2026
forecasts.note: OPENED today, and opened because this board was carrying a Brent barrier question that depends on a pipeline it had no question about. Separate the facts by class, because the whole forecast lives in the gap. CONFIRMED: Tuesday's Houthi missile and drone assault on southern Saudi Arabia injured at least 73 and set oil facilities ablaze, including the 400,000 barrel-a-day Jazan refinery. OBSERVED: Sentinel-3 imagery and NASA fire-detection data show a plume reported at 60 to 100 kilometres along the pipeline route southeast of Medina, with fire radiative power above 70 megawatts sustained more than eight hours - roughly double a conventional fire. UNCONFIRMED: that the pipeline itself was hit. Aramco has said nothing and Reuters cannot verify it. The anchor is the base rate and the two closest precedents point OPPOSITE ways: in May 2019 Houthi drones struck this same line at Afif and Aramco publicly confirmed a fire and a brief halt, which resolves the confirmation limb YES; in September 2019 Abqaiq removed about 5.7 million barrels a day, roughly half of Saudi output, and Aramco did NOT declare force majeure, delivering from storage to protect its reliability franchise, which resolves the force-majeure limb NO. Splitting those and discounting for a wartime information environment in which Aramco has now been silent for more than a day gives 40. Kill: the plume is attributed to a non-pipeline fire, or Aramco publishes normal Yanbu loading programmes through October, sends this to 15.

forecasts.q: Front-month Brent settles at or above $120/bbl on any daily settle before 31 Dec 2026
forecasts.note: CUT 7, and the move is arithmetic rather than opinion - which is the only kind of large move this book allows itself. Brent traded $104.53 live at 12:58Z against the $107.63 settle this question was opened on last night, and the vintage is published because the board's data vintage is a property of the board and not of the world. That widens the barrier from 11.5 to 13.8 per cent in log terms with 111 days to run. Recomputing the first-passage probability with futures treated as driftless gives 44 per cent at 35 per cent annualised volatility and 54 per cent at 45 per cent, against 54 and 63 last night. The published method takes the lower leg and trims two points for demand destruction and OPEC+ spare capacity, which lands on 42. Three points are added back for one thing a driftless diffusion structurally cannot see: a fire burning over the route of the pipeline that is the reason crude is not already higher. Kill unchanged: ten consecutive settles below $95 sends this to 25.

forecasts.q: The FOMC raises the fed funds target range at or before the 9-10 December 2026 meeting
forecasts.note: RAISED 7, the largest move of the session, and it is bought with an INVERTED OFFSET rather than with a new fact - which is why it is worth more than the two points the offset itself cost. Yesterday this desk held at 65 and named the reason: core producer prices at 0.2 per cent against 0.3 expected were 'the single number still saying energy rather than general inflation'. Today that number reversed. August core CPI rose 0.3 per cent on the month against 0.2 expected, an acceleration from July, while headline printed 3.4 per cent against a 3.3 per cent consensus with gasoline supplying more than a third of the monthly rise. An offset that bought two points when it held should pay more than two when it inverts. What holds this at 72 rather than 88 is the honest half of the same release: core CPI on the YEAR fell to 2.4 per cent from 2.5, which is the Blinder and Bernanke look-through case stated in the data itself - a committee can read this as energy passing through a core still converging on target. Anchor held at 50. Kill unchanged: holds at both 16 September and 4-5 November with the dissent bloc shrinking sends this to 45.

forecasts.q: Major US and/or Israeli strike campaign on Iran resumes (multi-day, state targets)
forecasts.note: CUT 3 on revealed preference, against yesterday's raise on rhetoric. Mohammed bin Salman called the president twice on Thursday asking for American strikes on the Houthis and was refused; CENTCOM's Adm. Brad Cooper flew to Riyadh for coordination instead, the US will supply intelligence and targeting data, about 200 American personnel are already in the kingdom in non-kinetic roles, and a senior official framed the policy as empowering regional partners to take the lead. The obvious objection is faced rather than dodged: this is the Houthi file, not the Iran file, and this book has refused points for exactly that mismatch before. It is admitted because it is an ACTION by the same principal in the same week on the same underlying question - appetite for new kinetic commitments in this theatre - where yesterday's two points were bought with a QUOTE at a party convention. Allison's third model is the mechanism: where you sit is where you stand, and a president who declines a treaty partner's direct request during an attack on that partner's territory is showing the coalition's real price. Capped at 3 because refusing to bomb Ansar Allah is entirely consistent with striking Iran directly.

forecasts.q: USD/JPY appreciates 8 per cent or more from 160.0 (to 147.2 or below) in any rolling 30 days
forecasts.note: RAISED 2, and the finding is the VINTAGE rather than the two points. The three-session data gap is closed: USD/JPY is 153.42 live, corroborated at 154.18 on an independent 10 September fix, against the FRED print of 156.11 dated 4 September that this desk twice refused to mark on. That refusal can now be scored as correct - the stale number was wrong in the wrong direction, and marking from it would have walked the book AWAY from the barrier while spot walked toward it. The daily series runs 160.20 down to 153.42 over about seven sessions. The resolution criterion is pinned in advance, without rewriting the question: the barrier is 147.20, and the rolling-30-day clause requires the 8 per cent decline to complete within 30 calendar days of a print at or above 160.0. The two readings currently almost coincide, since 8 per cent below the trailing 30-day high of 160.20 is 147.38 - so the ambiguity is pinned before it becomes material. Only two points because the last LIVE mark, on 7 September, used 154.06 and produced 29; spot has moved 0.4 per cent since. Barrier arithmetic to the early-October window expiry: 13 per cent at 10.5 per cent implied volatility, 32 per cent at the roughly 16 per cent realised over seven sessions. The BOJ on 18 September is the confirmation leg.

forecasts.q: Saudi Arabia publicly announces enrichment, weapons pursuit, or a nuclear-sharing arrangement
forecasts.note: RAISED 3, and this is the pathway logged-but-not-paid yesterday finally arriving with evidence of its own kind. Yesterday this desk refused to spend points on Pakistan's statement that the Mecca pact would be made operational, because that is a CONVENTIONAL guarantee and this question resolves on enrichment, weapons pursuit or nuclear sharing. Today's input is different in kind: the patron itself declined. Sagan's security model of proliferation runs on precisely this observable - a client hedges when the credibility of its guarantee falls, not when the threat rises - and today the threat and the credibility moved in opposite directions within hours of each other. The base rate governs the size and it is the reason this is 18 rather than 30: South Korea in the 1970s, Japan through the 1990s and Taiwan after 1979 all hedged quietly after larger credibility shocks, and none of them announced. Announcement is the rarest step in the sequence, which is what this question is written on.

forecasts.q: US diesel crack spread settles back below $45/bbl before 15 Dec 2026
forecasts.note: CUT 2 on a confirmation upgrade. Last night The War Zone could not confirm the capture of Perim; today four Yemeni government sources told Reuters the Houthis reached the island after government forces withdrew, with Dhubab taken opposite it. The Red Sea distillate arbitrage - Hirschman's substitutability condition, which was the basis of the 10 September cut - is now degraded on confirmed rather than reported facts. Capped at two by a counter-mechanism this desk should state out loud rather than bury: a CRUDE supply shock COMPRESSES cracks, because a crack spread is product minus crude. If Petroline is genuinely impaired, crude rises against product and pushes this question toward YES. The two effects have opposite signs and only one of them is confirmed, which is exactly the situation in which a small move is the honest one.

forecasts.q: Israel-Hezbollah escalates to a multi-week campaign
forecasts.note: CUT 2 on the FRAMING of a very large kinetic act, which is the sort of move that looks wrong on the day and right on the month. Israel destroyed a Hezbollah subterranean complex on the Ali al-Taher ridge using a reported 1,000 tonnes of explosives, producing a tremor read at magnitude 4.1 - and Netanyahu and Katz described the operation as COMPLETING the consolidation of the security zone. Schelling's distinction governs: an operation publicised as consummating a limited objective is a price being banked, not a campaign being opened. Demolition inside a zone already held, announced as finished, is weak evidence for a multi-week campaign however loud the day was. Capped at two because Israel simultaneously said it stands ready for further strikes, and because engineering work at this scale can be the covering action for the posture that precedes an offensive.

forecasts.q: Hormuz transits recover to more than 50 per cent of pre-war volume by 25 Nov 2026
forecasts.note: HELD at 10, on its floor, for a SIXTH instance of the same pattern. The FT reports Gulf foreign ministers will meet their Iranian counterpart on Monday in Salalah to seek buy-in for a temporary deal to MANAGE shipping through the strait, and oil slipped on the report. This book's standing rule is that an announcement is not a transit, and it has now been applied six times since the June memorandum lapsed. The transit print still governs and still points the other way: seven Hormuz transits on Wednesday against a ten-day average of 14, on a question that needs roughly 65 a day. A clock was added rather than points. Note what a deal to MANAGE shipping would actually do to this book: it is the precise shape GEO-013 predicts, transit machinery preserved under a new name.

hypotheses.name: IRGC captured the succession (weak form — assessed finding)
hypotheses.d: Documented pressure on Assembly electors, 8 boycotts, overridden shortlist and will. The pre-arranged-pact version scores only 30% — the plan was overridden, not executed.

hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — HELD 82%
hypotheses.d: HELD. The promised authenticated footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders still has not landed, so the falsifier remains un-run. The week was IRGC-forward — the Guard, not the foreign ministry, confirmed it ran the Oman channel and announced the revenue-sharing terms, and the Guard made the mine-strike claim — but that is DENIED as a raise under the shared-prediction rule: 'the Guard runs the maritime file' is predicted just as strongly by an ordinary reading in which the IRGC is a powerful institution under a functioning Supreme Leader, which is a much weaker claim than 'the IRGC rules Iran'. The 82% cap stands for exactly the reason it was set.

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Held at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: Nobody's hurrying on Hormuz — 60% → 65% (RAISED)
hypotheses.d: Its first fact that BEATS a rival instead of merely fitting itself. On 30 Aug the US struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak after observing Guard personnel preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the strait — two days after CENTCOM declared the lanes fully cleared, and while Muscat negotiates a minesweeping calendar. The 08-30 audit had installed a genuine rival — a physical clock, minesweeping simply takes time — and ruled this hypothesis must beat it. A physical clock runs down; this one is being rewound, by the exact actor the hypothesis named in advance. Capped at +5 on three counts kept in front: CENTCOM is the interested party and 'observed preparations' is unpublished intelligence used to justify a strike; Al Jazeera published a technical challenge on 31 Aug to whether Iran can even mine by rocket as claimed; and IRGC counter-coercion against a blockade that has redirected 83 vessels, disabled three and boarded two explains the same act without any rent motive. Not pre-event.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — HELD 60%, tell sharpened
hypotheses.d: August continues the signature: 125 PLA aerial ADIZ incursions (the 2026 decline intact) against 152 non-warship PRC vessels in the first 21 days, ~60% coast guard, with the east-of-Taiwan patrols now a declared 'new normal'. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up. NOT moved — this is the same signal that bought +5 on 08-26, and re-marking on the continuation of its own evidence is the double-count the audit named. The important item is against my own test: if Beijing has DECLARED the patrols permanent, their persistence through the Sept 24 visit is close to uninformative. Re-specified now, in advance and stricter — the informative observation on 09-23→09-25 is a boarding, an inspection, or a first-time-area incursion. Mere presence no longer counts as confirmation.

hypotheses.name: Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it holds at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Falsifiers: token export volumes, Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing not actually swinging off the Middle East, or the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appearing. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Note it is DISTINCT from 'The Portfolio State' below, which is about the vehicle rather than the motive.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — HELD 52%
hypotheses.d: Confirming but shared, therefore ambience: Treasury again held back on Chinese financial institutions, with mainstream reporting now naming the mechanism outright — designating them 'could create tensions before Xi's visit'. Bessent's promised weekly cadence hit banks but no Chinese one, and at the G20 he pushed severing Iran financial ties while China dissented. Both the leverage read and the ordinary 'Washington won't detonate its own summit' read predict all of it. The strongest weekly argument AGAINST, logged rather than absorbed: the US struck Iran on three consecutive nights and took Iranian fire onto three Arab host states. Deliberate slow-walking for leverage sits badly with sustained kinetic escalation that raises the cost of the thing being slow-walked — that counterweight is what holds the number at 52.

hypotheses.name: A pre-announcement leak into oil futures — 40% → 34% (biggest mover)
hypotheses.d: Its lead conditional has now gone unfired across three weeks containing the most violently market-moving Iran news since April — the 30 Aug Larak strike, three nights of exchanges, two struck VLCCs, Brent to ~$95 — with not one reported nine-figure pre-announcement episode. The file is confirmed as historical and bounded: DOJ is probing four trades totalling ~$2.6bn, all inside a five-week window that closed in April — Mar 23 (>$500m, ~15 min before Trump's delay post), Apr 7 ($960m before the ceasefire), Apr 17 ($760m, ~20 min before Iran said Hormuz was open), Apr 21 ($430m before the extension). CORRECTION BANKED AGAINST THIS ENTRY: the ledger's earlier '~$2.2bn cluster' for Mar 23 and its '~$7bn' aggregate are both withdrawn as over-wide constructions. The cut is made on the hypothesis's own written terms, not on a preferred reading — a conditional set at 60% has burned three of fourteen weeks in the best environment it will ever get and produced nothing. The cut is only −6 because of one genuinely new structural fact: investigators are running a SEPARATE probe into prediction-market activity on the same developments, and the same foreknowledge reaching two unrelated venues is hard to explain as one market-maker hedging client flow. Split now: deliberate leak 34 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 36 / coincidence 10. Still the only entry whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event.

hypotheses.name: NEW · The Portfolio State — coercion converted into sovereign equity, statute retrofitted
hypotheses.d: Strongest form: the US is converting military and sanctions leverage into permanent state equity in strategic supply chains, with the legal authority written to fit transactions rather than the reverse — Venezuela being the first hydrocarbon use of a template already run in chips and critical minerals. The rail predates the headline, which is the only thing licensing a design read at all: Senate NDAA FY2027 §1051 was marked up in MID-JUNE — ten weeks before the 29 Aug deal — creating a DoD Equity Investment Account, authorising OSC equity to $500m and capping any single position at 40% of the entity; the Venezuela stake is 35%, inside a cap that does not legally exist yet. Add DoD's own $400m/15% stake in MP Materials with 100% offtake (structurally identical to Venezuela's '20% of output at cost'), House Oversight already demanding an accounting of Venezuelan oil revenue on 23 Feb, and CFR's tally of 26 government equity deals worth ~$23.9bn. It opens at only 25% because the boring, incompetence and patronage readings are all strong: think tanks have been publicly naming and counting this pattern since 2025 (a policy, not a plot); the Pentagon's own spokesman flatly DENIES that OSC takes equity while WSJ reports it doing so, which is improvisation not design; and a 100-year concession over 65bn bbl routed to one politically connected operator with no published contract is better explained as spoils allocation. Above all the base rate is enormous — Anglo-Persian 1914, the RFC, GM/Chrysler 2009 — so the design premium must be small. NOT a conspiracy claim and must never be scored as one: it requires no secrecy at all, only anticipation, and the honest gap is that I cannot name the operator who executes the warrants. Key test: does the ENACTED NDAA widen §1051 beyond critical minerals to energy, or raise the cap, by 31 Dec (45%)? Scope enacted unchanged kills the design read.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 25% → 22% (CUT, sixth session running)
hypotheses.d: The week finally produced Russia-Iran material and it is the wrong KIND. Moscow said publicly on 01 Sep that air defence is the main focus of military-technical cooperation with Iran, alongside a reported 500 Verba MANPADS and 2,500 missiles and continued fighter deliveries. That is the resupply leg — already priced at 7/10 under 'means'. It moves nothing: it is announced by TASS, an interested party publishing its own helpfulness and the structural opposite of a covert channel; the opportunism branch predicts arms sales to a client at war identically, so under the standing rule it is ambience; and after six sessions there is still ZERO documentary evidence Moscow has influenced Tehran's negotiating position, which is the actual claim. Arms transfers are not persuasion. Cut rather than held because a decay rule that bites only on its deadline is a cliff, not decay. Clock unchanged: 15% on 30 Sep absent documentary evidence, retire below 10%.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Nothing resolved this week, and one file addition cuts against it: the summit's Iran content is now openly reported as an explicit US ask — Chinese pressure on Tehran to reopen the strait — with Beijing expected to want Taiwan concessions in return. An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: Houthis declare the Red Sea safe for all but Saudi ships
brief.h: Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said maritime navigation in the Red Sea 'is safe, except for Saudi ships', and vowed to escalate against Saudi forces until the blockade of Yemen is lifted - hours after Ansar Allah completed its takeover of Yemen's entire western coast, seizing Dhubab, the Hanish islands, Zuqar and Perim and claiming 5,400 square kilometres in under a day.
brief.t: Read the sentence as an instrument rather than as reassurance, because that is what it is. A general closure of Bab el-Mandeb would summon exactly the navies Ansar Allah has spent two years learning to avoid; a named exemption list summons nobody and still strangles one counterparty. That is the difference between a blockade and an embargo, and it is the whole story: Saudi crude has been going west since the Iran war shut Hormuz - pumped across the peninsula to Yanbu on the Red Sea, then out past Yemen - and today the exit was declared closed to Saudi hulls alone. The tell that it is working is not gunfire but routing. Lloyd's List Intelligence reports Yanbu cargoes that previously transited the Red Sea are increasingly going NORTH through Suez instead, which is the long, dear way to the same customers.
brief.context: The rail is older than the militia. Perim, thirteen square kilometres of volcanic rock less than two miles off the Yemeni coast, splits the strait into two channels and carries a runway of roughly 6,150 feet built by the UAE in 2021 during its own Yemen intervention - infrastructure built by one belligerent and inherited by another, which is why retaking it is now an order of magnitude dearer. The deciding desk is Ansar Allah's military command and, per Reuters and The National citing intercepted communications, senior IRGC officers including Abdolreza Shahlaei sent to oversee the campaign; Tehran denies giving direction. The base rate is the discipline here: holding one bank of a strait has never been the same as closing one - Egypt held a bank of Suez from 1967 and Iran has sat on Hormuz for four decades, and in both cases the traffic effect ran through insurance and routing rather than gunfire. The tracked numbers say repricing, not closure: 302 transits through Bab el-Mandeb in the week to 23 August with 257 AIS-traceable, then 202 traceable the following week, against a pre-ban weekly average of 319. The falsifier has still not happened and is specific - verified imagery of anti-ship missiles, radar or aircraft emplaced on the Perim airstrip. A capture is a headline; an emplacement is a closure.

angles.effect: GAINS the most valuable thing a chokepoint force can hold - the ability to price one customer out of a lane without giving any navy a casus belli, which is a revenue and leverage position rather than a siege
PAYS directly: with Hormuz shut and the southern Red Sea exit declared hostile to its flag, its seaborne crude has to go north through Suez at longer voyage and higher war-risk premium, or not at all
GAIN only what the insurance market is willing to price - a belligerent's safe-conduct is not a legal guarantee, and the 202-transit week shows owners already discounting it
PAY with displacement - Médecins Sans Frontières reports mass movement out of Mokha and hospital staff leaving

dec.kill: A non-Saudi-flagged hull struck or seized in the strait. That would convert the carve-out into a lie and make this a general closure, which is a different story with a different response.

consp.claim: That this is the opening move of a full US-Iran war - a 97-reply all-caps thread argues the closure of a second strait, one feeding directly into Suez, drives oil past $500 and plunges Europe into darkness before winter. A parallel and much larger thread runs the opposite way, arguing the episode proves 'America is a failed state' because the world's largest military cannot stop barefoot irregulars from shutting oil shipping. A smaller thread claims the Houthis took the ground by generating an AI deepfake of an enemy commander ordering a retreat, calling it 'the cheapest landgrab in the entirety of human history'.
consp.spread: A 97-reply /pol/ 'WW3 IMMINENT' thread, a 134-reply failed-state thread, the 264-reply Persia-Israel general carrying the territorial claims as headline items, and a small deepfake thread
consp.read: Two frames fighting over one event, and it is worth noticing they cannot both be right: the same board argues the US is about to be dragged in AND that it is too weak to intervene. The checkable kernel under the deepfake claim is that Yemeni government forces did withdraw from Perim and Dhubab before the fighting rather than during it, which is genuinely unexplained and is what the story is filling in - a collapse without a battle invites an exotic cause. The $500 figure has no mechanism attached; routing disruption is not lost production, and barrels going the long way round are still barrels.

brief.head: Gulf ministers will meet Iran in Oman to seek a Hormuz deal
brief.h: Foreign ministers of the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council are to meet Iran's Abbas Araghchi in the Omani city of Salalah on Monday in an Omani-brokered push for an interim arrangement managing shipping through the Strait of Hormuz - the first meeting between GCC top diplomats and a senior Iranian official since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in February.
brief.t: The concession is the attendance, not the text. Iran has blockaded Hormuz since 28 February; it currently requires vessels to seek permission before transiting and, per Iranian officials, is weighing a mechanism to charge service fees. Turning up to negotiate the terms of that permission is how a blockade becomes an administration - and an administered waterway with a fee schedule is a far more durable asset than a closed one, because everybody who pays acquires an interest in the arrangement continuing. Name the mechanism and it stops being novel: the Danish crown charged the Sound Dues on every ship entering the Baltic for four hundred years, and it survived that long because the payers preferred a predictable toll to an unpredictable strait.
brief.context: Tehran and Muscat said just over two weeks ago they were finalising a temporary arrangement under which vessels enter the strait through Iranian waters and exit mostly through Omani territory - which is the shape of the thing: sovereignty split, transit administered, both administrators paid. The deciding desk is not the GCC secretariat; it is Oman's foreign ministry, which has brokered every Iran channel since the 2013 back-channel, plus Araghchi and whoever in Tehran can hold the Revolutionary Guards to a text. Diplomats caution that full reopening requires a US-Iran agreement the GCC cannot deliver, so what Monday can realistically produce is a partial, deniable modus vivendi. The base rate is unkind to the optimistic read and kind to the durable one: interim maritime arrangements that create an administrator almost never get unwound - they get renamed. This desk has held at 76 per cent since August that any deal preserves Iranian transit-administration machinery in some form, and Monday is the first scheduled test that question has ever had. What would change it is a published text that removes the permit requirement rather than rebranding it.

angles.effect: GAINS the thing sanctions were meant to deny it - a legal-looking permit regime over a waterway, negotiated with the neighbours who are supposed to be containing it, plus a revenue line that never touches the banking system
GAINS indispensability: every arrangement that routes exits through Omani water makes Muscat a party to world oil logistics rather than a bystander
PAY in precedent - showing up concedes that transit through a strait they border is something to be arranged with Tehran, which is the recognition Iran has sought since 1979
PAYS leverage: a regional deal that does not need the US is a deal the US cannot price, and it weakens the argument that only an American-brokered settlement reopens the strait
GAIN modestly - a published rule, even a rule written by a belligerent, is cheaper to underwrite than an unpublished one

dec.kill: A published text in which transit requires no Iranian permission and no fee. Absent that, the deal is the machinery, whatever it ends up being called.

consp.claim: That the war is being deliberately extended because American energy producers are the beneficiaries, pointing at a Brown University real-time tracker finding Americans have paid an extra $102 billion for petrol and diesel since the Iran war began, and posting it as 'Trump Boosts Fuel Industry By $100 Billion'. Related threads treat any negotiated Hormuz arrangement as theatre timed to the midterms rather than a genuine attempt to reopen the strait.
consp.spread: A /pol/ thread built on a WFLA writeup of the Brown tracker, feeding into the 287-reply Trump general and the running Persia-Israel thread
consp.read: This is the cui bono fallacy with a real number attached, which is what makes it travel: the $102bn figure is a genuine sourced estimate of consumer cost, and consumer cost is producer revenue. What it cannot establish is authorship. The disconfirming fact sits on the same page - an administration absorbing record pump prices five weeks before a midterm is paying a political cost no designer of the scheme would choose, which is why this desk prices deliberate American slow-walking at only 52 per cent rather than higher.

brief.head: CIA releases the Al Qaeda warnings it sent Clinton and Bush
brief.h: On the twenty-fifth anniversary of the attacks, the New York Times reports the CIA has published intelligence the agency passed to the Clinton and Bush White Houses about Al Qaeda before 11 September 2001 - the latest movement in a declassification push the Public Interest Declassification Board pressed on the President in a letter of 30 June 2026.
brief.t: The story is the machinery, not the paper. Two sets of records the 9/11 Commission explicitly wanted public have been stuck for two decades: the President's Daily Brief summary of what was known before the attacks, and the Memorandums for the Record of the Commission's interviews with Condoleezza Rice, Sandy Berger, Richard Clarke, Michael Scheuer and George Tenet. Those are now before ISCAP - the Interagency Security Classification Appeals Panel, the small interagency body with the power to overrule an agency that refuses to declassify its own embarrassment. Anniversaries are when that machinery moves, and the reason is unglamorous: ISCAP is a political instrument as much as a legal one, and the cost of a refusal rises on the day the cameras are pointed at it. Carried openly - this desk has verified the declassification track and the Board's record, but has not independently read today's tranche.
brief.context: The base rate on this file is brutal and worth holding before anyone calls today a revelation: the 6 August 2001 brief titled 'Bin Laden Determined to Strike in US' was written seven weeks before the attacks and was not released until April 2004, and it took a commission, a subpoena fight and a sitting president's consent to get four pages out. The Public Interest Declassification Board said on 1 September that it 'remains fully committed to ensuring that the U.S. government honors the 9/11 Commission's stated intent that the records of its work should be declassified', and that the records 'are now under review' by ISCAP - which is a status, not a release. The deciding desk is therefore ISCAP and the equity-holding agencies, not the CIA press office, and the variable that decides whether this matters is redaction density rather than page count. What would change the read is the Memorandums for the Record appearing substantially unredacted, because the MFRs are where officials said under questioning what the sanitised report only implies.

angles.effect: GAINS a cheap transparency win on the one day of the year when the audience is guaranteed, without conceding control of what stays redacted
PAY little - staged release through ISCAP lets equity holders shape sequencing and redaction, which converts a reckoning into a managed drip
GAIN real primary material, and simultaneously LOSE leverage: a withheld document is a campaign, a released and redacted one is a closed file

angles.party: Anyone named in the Memorandums for the Record
angles.effect: PAYS reputationally in proportion to how little is blacked out - which is precisely why the redaction line is the decision

dec.kill: The PDB summary and the five Memorandums for the Record published substantially unredacted. That would make this a declassification rather than a commemoration.

consp.claim: The anniversary has put the full catalogue back on the board at volume. The largest thread argues that pre-attack insider trading - put options on the airlines, and the career of a former Marsh & McLennan employee at the World Trade Center - proves the operation was run above the level of any single state, 'Rothschild-tier'. Others assert flatly that it was an inside job and that everyone knew in advance and let it happen; a long-running thermodynamics thread reruns the jet-fuel-versus-structural-steel melting-point argument; and a counter-thread titled 'Al-Qaeda did 9/11 and I'm tired of pretending they didn't' is itself doing numbers. Separately, several high-traffic threads run an ethnic-scapegoat narrative asserting a named religious group planned and executed the attacks, citing the existence of an FBI file on five men detained in 2001 and a trademark filing made shortly after the first impact.
consp.spread: A 193-reply insider-trading thread, a 134-reply thread complaining about '9/11 defenders', a 197-reply everything-is-a-lie thread, a 29-reply Al-Qaeda-did-it counter-thread, an /x/ predictive-programming and occult general, and a run of smaller scapegoat threads
consp.read: The insider-trading claim is the interesting one because it has a checkable kernel: the 9/11 Commission investigated the options activity specifically and traced the largest positions to ordinary institutional hedging, which is a finding people are entitled to distrust but not to ignore. The scapegoat variant is reported here as a phenomenon and its content is not repeated; the technique is the oldest in the catalogue - cite a real document, then treat its EXISTENCE as confirmation of what it does not say, since an investigative file records that something was investigated, which is the opposite of a finding. The genuine kernel under all of it, and the reason today's release lands in this environment, is that the government did withhold this material for twenty-five years, and prolonged official secrecy manufactures the demand that fills the vacuum.

brief.head: Xi heads to Delhi with 400 officials after a seven-year freeze
brief.h: China's foreign ministry confirmed Xi Jinping will attend the 18th BRICS summit in New Delhi on 12-13 September, his first visit to India in nearly seven years, travelling with a delegation of about 400 officials against fewer than 200 in 2019, and calling for a 'strategic' and 'long-term' view of ties; Delhi police detained five people for raising anti-Xi slogans near the venue.
brief.t: The delegation size is the signal and the summit is the pretext. Four hundred officials is a working headcount - ministries, customs, civil aviation, standards bodies - and you do not fly that many people in to co-sign a communique. What moved is not sentiment but arithmetic: American tariff policy has made the China hedge cheaper for Delhi than it has been since the 2020 Galwan clash, and Beijing is buying the opening at exactly the moment it is cheapest. Follow the incentive rather than the summit branding - BRICS provides the room and the photograph, but the bargain being negotiated is strictly bilateral, and its currency is flights, visas, customs clearances and rare-earth supply rather than anything in the declaration.
brief.context: Xi's last India visit was the informal Mamallapuram summit with Modi in 2019; the Galwan Valley killings in June 2020 froze the relationship, direct flights, most visa categories and Chinese investment approvals together, and the thaw has been running in small increments since. The deciding desk is the Indian Prime Minister's Office and the Chinese foreign ministry, not the BRICS chair - and the constraint Delhi cannot legislate away is that China supplies the processed rare earths and specialty chemicals Indian manufacturing runs on, which is leverage that survives any summit mood. The base rate is the sobering one: every India-China thaw since 1988 has held until the next line-of-actual-control incident, and the LAC is unmarked by design. Watch what a Modi-Xi bilateral readout actually names. A restored direct-flight schedule, a visa category reopened, or a named rare-earth supply commitment would be new; another endorsement of a 'strategic and long-term view' would be the fifteenth of its kind.

angles.effect: GAINS the highest-value outcome available to it this year - visible daylight between Washington and its most important Indo-Pacific partner, bought with trade concessions rather than concessions on the border
GAINS leverage in its own tariff negotiation with Washington and a partial hedge on inputs it cannot source elsewhere; PAYS by normalising with a state that still holds contested ground
PAYS the bill for its own tariff policy - the push factor here is American, and no amount of Quad architecture offsets a price signal Indian exporters feel every month
GAINS a summit photograph in which it is not isolated, at the price of hosting a bloc whose two largest members sit on opposite sides of the Iran war

angles.party: Tibetan and Uyghur diaspora protesters in India
angles.effect: PAY immediately and visibly - five detained for slogans near the venue is the cost of the visit being smooth

dec.kill: A Modi-Xi bilateral that produces no named deliverable, or a fresh LAC incident. Either returns the relationship to its 2020 baseline within a news cycle.

consp.claim: That Washington engineered the India-China rapprochement, deliberately or through incompetence - that the tariff campaign against Delhi was either a handover of India to Beijing by a captured administration, or proof the US no longer has an Asia strategy at all. Separately, an ethnic-scapegoat narrative about Indians is running as the single highest-reply thread on the board today, unconnected to the summit but colouring every India thread beneath it.
consp.spread: India-related threads across /pol/ including the day's top thread by reply count, with the summit itself getting comparatively little direct attention
consp.read: The strategic claim has a real kernel and a false inference. The kernel: tariff pressure on India is genuine, measurable, and is plausibly the largest single push factor behind Delhi's warming to Beijing - the Wall Street Journal made the same argument today from the establishment side. The inference to intent is the cui bono slide again; policy that produces a bad second-order outcome is the ordinary output of governments optimising for a domestic audience. The scapegoat thread is logged as a phenomenon and its content is not repeated - note the technique, which is to park a degrading generalisation about a nationality at the top of the catalogue so that every substantive thread about that country is read through it.

brief.head: Mexico races Washington for a tariff deal before the midterms
brief.h: Six sources in both countries told Reuters that Mexico and the United States are sprinting toward an interim bilateral bargain before the 3 November midterms, trading relief from Section 232 tariffs - currently 50 per cent on steel and aluminium and 25 per cent on vehicles - for American demands on automotive content and on screening Chinese investment in Mexico.
brief.t: The machine under this headline is the quiet dismantling of USMCA. A trilateral treaty renegotiated one party at a time is not a treaty any more; it is a hub-and-spoke system in which the hub sets terms and the spokes cannot coordinate. Canada tested the alternative last month, its talks collapsed, and Washington answered with tariffs on Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and dairy. Mexico watched that and chose accommodation - a Mexico-based source described the strategy to Reuters as 'play nice and continue to cooperate'. Follow what is actually being bought: Washington is not principally buying cars, it is buying a Chinese-investment firewall on its southern border that it would struggle to legislate at home, and Mexico is paying for tariff relief in the currency of its own investment-screening law.
brief.context: Mexico sends more than 80 per cent of its exports to the United States, which is not a trading relationship but a dependency, and it is the reason the negotiating asymmetry is total. The terms under discussion mirror what was offered to Ottawa: a 15 per cent vehicle tariff with an additional reduction for American content, bringing the effective rate to roughly 7 per cent - against the 15 per cent that Japan, the EU and South Korea already pay and the 10 per cent Britain pays. The deciding desks are USTR Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who met President Claudia Sheinbaum virtually on Thursday, against Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard - and Sheinbaum's binding constraint is not politics but credit, with Mexican ratings sliding and the deal serving as market reassurance. The base rate on pre-election trade announcements is that they are frameworks rather than ratified instruments; the object that would settle it is a Federal Register notice adjusting the Section 232 rate, because a proclamation changing a tariff schedule is binding and a joint statement is not.

angles.effect: GAINS a pre-midterm trade win plus a China-screening regime on its border written into Mexican law rather than American law, which is cheaper and harder to repeal
GAINS tariff relief and a ratings-agency story; PAYS with sovereignty over its own foreign-investment approvals, now shaped to an external demand
PAYS the most and is not in the room - a bilateral Mexico deal strands Ottawa's refusal and makes the trilateral review a formality
PAY directly: the proposed Mexican legislation to review and block foreign acquisitions is aimed at them by construction
GAIN cheaper integrated supply chains relative to today's rates, while the content rules push cost back toward American engines, electronics and software

dec.kill: A Federal Register notice actually adjusting Mexico's Section 232 rate. Until that appears this is a framework, and importers are still paying 50 and 25 per cent.

consp.claim: That the tariff revenue figures being cited by the administration are fabricated - a thread built on a viral post mocking a claim that '21 trillion' has been collected in tariffs argues the numbers are invented outright to justify the policy, and that the real transfer is from American consumers to the Treasury with the incidence hidden inside retail prices.
consp.spread: A 77-reply /biz/ thread on a viral X post, running alongside the board's diesel and inflation threads
consp.read: The mockery is aimed at an obviously garbled number, but the economics being gestured at underneath are the mainstream finding rather than a fringe one: tariffs are collected from importers and the incidence falls substantially on domestic buyers, which is why a tariff wall and a record diesel print sit on the same board and get argued about separately. The fabrication claim is the weak half and the incidence claim is the strong one - and the checkable object is Treasury's monthly customs duty line, which is published.

watch: Monday's Salalah text, not Monday's photograph. The question is whether any arrangement removes the Iranian permit requirement or merely renames it - this desk has held the rename at 76 per cent since August and has never had a scheduled test of it before.

Verified imagery of anti-ship missiles, radar or aircraft emplaced on the Perim airstrip. Holding a strait and closing one are different things, and the UAE-built 6,150-foot runway is where the difference becomes visible.

lesson: Today is the twenty-fifth anniversary of 11 September, the boards are saturated with it, and the technique on display is one worth being able to name, because you will meet it in serious analysis too. Call it the CUI BONO FALLACY - the slide from 'who benefited?' to 'therefore who did it'. Asking who benefits is not the error; it is compulsory, and this desk runs it on every story, which is why each brief card carries a ledger of who gains and who pays. The error is treating benefit as evidence of authorship, because benefit is downstream of an event and almost everything that happens benefits somebody. The reason it feels so persuasive is that it is unfalsifiable in the direction it is offered: if the beneficiary did it, that proves the theory, and if the beneficiary denies it, that is what a beneficiary would do - and a claim that no observation can damage has stopped being a claim about the world. Sunstein and Vermeule described the social machinery that sustains this as crippled epistemology, where a closed information circle supplies all the confirmations and none of the tests; the honest correction is Popper's, which is to ask in advance what would have to be true for you to drop it. Apply it to today's actual board and the discipline pays for itself immediately: American oil producers benefit enormously from a strait closed at both ends, and this desk still prices deliberate American slow-walking at only 52 per cent, because the same administration is absorbing record pump prices five weeks before a midterm election - a cost no designer of the plan would choose. And when the cui bono frame reaches for an ethnic or religious 'who', as several of the highest-traffic anniversary threads did today, it has stopped being sloppy reasoning and become the oldest persuasion technique there is: supplying a culprit whose guilt requires no evidence because the audience already believed it.

quiz.q: The brief says Houthi forces holding Perim gives them the ability to CONTEST the strait, not to control it. What makes that distinction real?
options: Perim is too small to base any weapon on
The western side of Bab el-Mandeb is Djibouti and Eritrea, so one force cannot hold both banks
International law forbids closing a strait, so control is impossible
The island has no runway or infrastructure
quiz.why: A strait has two banks. Ansar Allah now holds the Yemeni side and an island in the middle, which lets it price and threaten traffic - but Djibouti and Eritrea face it, so this is contestation rather than sovereign closure. The observable that would change the reading is hardware emplaced on Perim's UAE-built runway, not the capture itself.

quiz.q: Why does the brief treat Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as the load-bearing fact behind the oil price rather than a side story?
options: It is the only Saudi export route that does not pass through the Strait of Hormuz
It carries Iranian crude under a permit arrangement
It supplies American Gulf Coast refineries directly
It is the world's longest pipeline
quiz.why: Petroline runs crude from Abqaiq to Yanbu on the Red Sea, bypassing Hormuz entirely. It is the physical reason analysts could say crude was not already far higher. But a pipeline ends at a port, and that port now loads into a strait held at its southern gate - a bypass with a besieged exit.

quiz.q: August CPI is described as handing the Federal Reserve both arguments in one document. Which pair of numbers does that?
options: Headline 3.4 per cent and gasoline up 27.4 per cent
Core up 0.3 per cent on the MONTH, while core on the YEAR fell to 2.4 per cent
Diesel at $6.06 and petrol at $4.30
The thirty-year at 5.35 and the ten-year at 4.95
quiz.why: Monthly core accelerating says the energy shock is spreading into general prices, which argues for a hike. Annual core falling toward target says it is passing through, which is the Blinder and Bernanke look-through case. One release, two defensible decisions - which is why this desk prices a hike at 72 per cent rather than 90.

quiz.q: Saudi Arabia's crown prince asked for American strikes twice and was refused. Which framework does the brief use to price the CONSEQUENCE of that refusal?
options: Prospect theory - cornered regimes gamble
Sagan's security model - clients hedge when the credibility of a guarantee falls
Mulder's sanctions-as-siege
Hirschman's substitutability
quiz.why: Sagan's security model says proliferation hedging tracks the credibility of the protector's guarantee, not the size of the threat - and today those two moved in opposite directions. That is why the Saudi nuclear question rose three points. The base rate keeps it at 18 rather than higher: states hedge quietly far more often than they announce.

quiz.q: A widely shared post argues: 'American oil producers are making a fortune from the closed strait, so Washington wants it closed.' What is the strongest reason to be careful with that?
options: American producers are not actually profiting from higher oil prices
Benefit is downstream of an event, so it cannot by itself establish who caused it - and the same administration is absorbing record pump prices before a midterm
Governments never act on behalf of commercial interests
The claim cannot be checked at all, so it should be ignored
quiz.why: This is the cui bono fallacy in today's lesson. Asking who benefits is compulsory; treating benefit as proof of authorship is the error, because almost every event benefits somebody. The disconfirming fact here is concrete and dated: record pump prices five weeks before an election are a cost no designer of the plan would volunteer for - which is why this desk prices deliberate slow-walking at 52 per cent rather than treating it as established.

plumbing.epoch: E6, the 2008-2022 quantitative-easing rail in its unwind chapter, meeting E4, the 1973 security-for-barrels bargain - and today E4 was the one that moved. That bargain traded American security guarantees for dollar-priced oil, and its unstated assumption was that the guarantor would keep the sea lanes open and would show up when a client was attacked. Both halves of that assumption were tested in one day: a chokepoint changed hands, a fire burned over the only pipeline that routes around the other chokepoint, and the guarantor declined a treaty partner's direct request for strikes, offering intelligence and targeting data instead. The old rail: a security guarantee underwritten by a navy with forward basing. The new permit: the guarantee is now explicitly partial - freedom of navigation for the lane, but the land war behind it is the partner's problem - and that repricing is happening at the same moment the monetary half of the bargain is being asked to absorb a supply shock with a demand instrument.

sections.t: US diesel set an all-time record this week at $5.820 a gallon, and the crack spread — the refiner's fee for turning crude into something an engine can burn — printed an all-time $108 a barrel while Brent sat at an unremarkable $96. In the same week US missiles reportedly struck a tanker at Iran's Kharg Island anchorage, and Ukrainian drones held Russian refinery runs at 3.6m barrels a day, the lowest since May 2002.

Crude — the thing everyone photographs and embargoes — is behaving; refined product is not. A $108 crack means the market will pay more to convert a barrel than the barrel is worth: a fact about cokers and hydrotreaters, not about oil. Name the mechanism — the conversion bottleneck. The binding constraint is never the abundant input but the narrow step in the middle, which cannot be built on the timescale of a war or an election.

sections.h: Deep history I — Rockefeller never wanted the oil
sections.t: John D. Rockefeller owned almost no wells. He owned the refineries of Cleveland, and what he did with them in 1871 is the founding text of chokepoint economics. Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad chartered the South Improvement Company, and Rockefeller's terms inside it were breathtaking: the Erie, New York Central and Pennsylvania would pay the SIC a rebate of $1.06 on every barrel it shipped — and a drawback of $1.06 on every barrel shipped by refiners outside the club. He was paid when his rivals did business. The charter was repealed that April before a single transaction cleared, and Ida Tarbell's exposé later finished the job — but the insight outlived the scandal: crude is worthless until someone converts and moves it, and whoever owns the narrow step prices the wide one.

sections.h: Deep history II — the war decided at the still
sections.t: The largest test of this proposition was the Allied air war, fought inside the alliance before it was fought over Germany. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command believed in punishment: burn the cities, break the will. Carl Spaatz and Arthur Tedder pushed what Harris dismissed as panacea targets — oil. Germany had almost no crude. It had Bergius hydrogenation, synthetic fuel pressed from coal at Leuna, Pölitz and Brüx, plants too enormous to hide. The oil plan began in May 1944. Leuna alone absorbed 22 raids, 6,552 bomber sorties and 18,328 tons of bombs across a year, behind Europe's heaviest flak concentration. It worked anyway. German synthetic output fell from a peak of 316,000 tons a month to 107,000 in June 1944 and 17,000 by September. Aviation gasoline — the specific fraction, not oil in general — went from 175,000 tons in April to 5,000 in September: 97% gone in five months. From May 1944 Germany consumed more than it produced every month, and the stockpile was gone in six.

sections.h: Deep history II — the fuel, not the factories
sections.t: The detail that makes it unforgettable: over the same period Albert Speer drove German tank and aircraft PRODUCTION to its wartime peak. The Reich ended 1944 with more airframes than it could fly and more panzers than it could move — the factories were fine and the fuel was not. The US Strategic Bombing Survey — written by people with every reason to praise bombing in general — judged the oil and transport campaigns decisive and the city campaign not. Japan lost the same way: the July 1941 freeze is remembered as an oil embargo, but the fatal shortage was 100-octane aviation gasoline, a conversion capability Japan could not build.

sections.h: Deep history III — how the West stopped building stills
sections.t: Now the slow part. The last greenfield major refinery built in the United States was Marathon's Garyville, Louisiana: built 1973-76, online 1977, still running at 596,000 barrels a day. Fifty years, no new plants — and the base is now shrinking: about 132 operable refineries in January 2025 against more than 300 in 1981, with roughly 1.235m b/d of distillation capacity removed in seven recent closures and conversions, over 6.5% of the total. All of it while shale made America the largest crude producer in history at 13.86m b/d. The country built the well and stopped building the still. The capacity emigrated rather than vanished — Jamnagar runs 1.24m b/d, Dangote opened at 650,000 and plans 1.4m, China kept building — so the toll moved east and south, to jurisdictions happy to buy discounted sanctioned crude and sell the product back to the people imposing the sanctions.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: In all three cases the scarce thing is the transformation, and transformation capacity is inelastic over any politically relevant horizon: a new crude supplier takes a fortnight, a new hydrocracker takes five years and a billion dollars. Ukraine is now running the 1944 oil plan at a ten-thousandth of the cost, a drone flying 1,550km to Omsk doing what 6,552 B-17 sorties did to Leuna — Pape's denial thesis tested live. It breaks against me here: Germany had no crude and no neutral supplier, Russia has both, and a 24-year low in refining has not stopped Pokrovsk.

sections.h: The adjudication — Yergin and Blas vs Chris Miller
sections.t: THE ADJUDICATION — YERGIN AND BLAS versus CHRIS MILLER Yergin and Blas hold that energy chokepoints self-heal — inventories, bypass and rerouting absorb shocks forecast to be fatal — and they have been right about the barrel, Brent at $96 in a war that curtailed over 11m b/d. Chris Miller's Chip War argues the opposite for inputs that are not fungible: no reserve of fabs, no bypass for EUV, a decade to rebuild. The evidence splits them by step. Yergin and Blas won the crude argument; the crack is the market announcing the win does not survive one step downstream, because there is no strategic reserve of cokers — the US holds hundreds of millions of barrels of crude in the SPR and about a million barrels of distillate in the Northeast reserve, having stockpiled the input it cannot burn. Miller's case is still weaker in oil than in silicon: diesel is shippable in a way a fab's output is not, so refining heals in 12-24 months rather than 12-24 days.

OECD gasoline demand is in structural decline as EVs scale; diesel and jet demand are not, because trucks, ships, aircraft, mining and data-centre backup have no substitute. But a refinery makes every cut at once, so the economics that close Western refineries — falling gasoline — destroy the distillate capacity nobody meant to lose. A trap, not a cycle; confidence high. The bolder call, near 60%: by the mid-2030s the US is at once the world's largest crude exporter and a chronic net importer of middle distillates, and that buys a strategic PRODUCT reserve — legislated storage of diesel and jet, enacted after a winter shortage rather than before one. What keeps this honest is GEO-026: does the US diesel crack settle below $45 before 15 December 2026? It sits at 35%, so the house is 65% on regime rather than outage — and if the crack mean-reverts on the 2022 schedule, this is an elegant story about a spike, published as a miss.
